about: The strategic corridors register of Africa Infra Watch: Africa's main cross-border transport and energy corridors, cut into their pieces, with each piece's stage and who pays for, owns and builds it, each with its source. Kept by hand; see build_corridors.py for the rules.

corridors.name: Lobito Corridor
corridors.length_note: The Benguela Railway, Lobito to Luau; about 1,000 km more on the DR Congo line and about 830 km on the planned line into Zambia
corridors.status_note: The Benguela Railway has run under the Lobito Atlantic Railway concession since January 2024, and its USD 753 m debt package closed in July 2026. The DR Congo signed its line to Mota-Engil in August 2026; the new railway into Zambia has an AfDB loan approved but no builder yet.
corridors.summary: A railway from Angola's Atlantic port of Lobito to the copper and cobalt mines of DR Congo's Katanga and Zambia's Copperbelt: the 1,289 km Benguela Railway, the DR Congo's line on to Kolwezi and Lubumbashi, and a new line planned into Zambia.
corridors.strategic: The flagship of the G7's Partnership for Global Infrastructure and Investment and the EU's Global Gateway: Washington and Brussels' answer to Chinese-built infrastructure, meant to carry critical minerals west to the Atlantic rather than east to Chinese buyers through Dar es Salaam and Durban.

corridors.name: Lamu Port–South Sudan–Ethiopia Transport Corridor (LAPSSET)
corridors.length_note: No single official spine length. The LAPSSET Corridor Development Authority lists highways of 530 km (Lamu–Garissa–Isiolo), 505 km (Isiolo–Moyale–Hawassa) and 700 km (Isiolo–Lokichar–Nadapal–Torit–Juba); Reuters (Aug 2023) put the planned railway network at about 3,000 km.

cost.note: Approximate cost of the whole programme (port, roads, railway, pipelines, refinery, power plant, airports) as reported by Reuters in Aug 2023. Older estimates differ and there is no current official total.

corridors.status_note: Lamu's three berths are in service and on 3 Oct 2026 handled the port's largest single-vessel discharge (about 5,200 TEUs). The Garissa–Isiolo road was 64% built in April 2026 and the railway is still at feasibility stage. On 1 Oct 2026 President Ruto said Dangote had agreed to help build a Turkana–Lamu crude pipeline; Kenya's February 2026 oil plan relied on trucks and rail instead.
corridors.summary: A Kenyan-led corridor from a new deep-water port at Lamu through Garissa to Isiolo, branching north to Moyale on the Ethiopian border and north-west through Turkana to Nakodok on the South Sudan border. It bundles a port, highways, a planned standard gauge railway and a planned crude oil pipeline, with airports, resort cities and a refinery site at Lamu.
corridors.strategic: Kenya pitches LAPSSET as an additional route to the sea for Ethiopia, which relies on Djibouti, and as an export outlet for South Sudan, which ships its oil through Sudan. Its oil case weakened when Uganda chose the Tanzanian EACOP route; China's CCCC built the port and the Lamu–Garissa road, both paid for from Kenya's own budget.

corridors.name: Northern Corridor Standard Gauge Railway (Mombasa–Nairobi–Malaba–Kampala–Kigali)
corridors.length_note: Built: Mombasa–Nairobi 472 km and Nairobi–Naivasha 120 km. Planned: Naivasha–Kisumu about 264 km, Kisumu–Malaba about 107 km, Malaba–Kampala 272 km, then on to Kigali (no official total).

cost.note: PIDA PAP2 cost estimate for the Mombasa–Nairobi–Malaba–Kampala–Kigali line with the Malaba–Nimule–Juba branch.

corridors.status_note: Mombasa–Naivasha has run since 2017/2019 and made its first operating profit in FY2025/26 (reported Sept 2026). Kenya declared works on Naivasha–Kisumu–Malaba started on 1 Jul 2026 (CCCC/CRBC), but in Aug 2026 they were still at land acquisition and only KSh 30 bn of the KSh 502.9 bn needed is committed; Uganda's Malaba–Kampala line won IsDB approval in Jun 2026 and targets financial close in Nov 2026.
corridors.summary: A standard gauge railway from the port of Mombasa to Nairobi and Naivasha, built by China and in service, meant to continue via Kisumu to Malaba on the Uganda border, then to Kampala and on to Rwanda. It carries containers and passengers alongside the colonial-era metre-gauge line on East Africa's busiest trade route.
corridors.strategic: Kenya's line is China's flagship Belt and Road railway in East Africa: China Exim lent about USD 4.9 bn for Mombasa–Naivasha, then declined to fund the next leg, and Kenya converted those loans to yuan in Oct 2025. Uganda dropped its Chinese contractor for Turkey's Yapı Merkezi with Islamic, African and European export credit money, and the EU lists the route as a Global Gateway corridor.

corridors.name: Central Corridor Standard Gauge Railway (Dar es Salaam–Mwanza/Kigoma, with Burundi and Rwanda links)
corridors.length_note: Lots 1-2 Dar es Salaam–Makutupora 722 km; Lots 3-4 Makutupora–Isaka about 430 km; Lot 5 Isaka–Mwanza 249 km main line; Tabora–Kigoma 411 km (PIDA) or 506 km (government); Uvinza–Musongati 240 km main line; Isaka–Kigali 532-571 km planned. No official total.

cost.note: PIDA investment prospectus figure for the whole Central Corridor SGR network (Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, DRC links); press reports in 2026 cite about USD 10 bn for Tanzania's SGR.

corridors.status_note: Dar es Salaam–Dodoma–Makutupora has carried passengers since mid-2024 and freight since June 2025. Lots 3-5 to Mwanza are under construction after Standard Chartered arranged a USD 2.33 bn package (Apr 2026), and President Samia laid the Tabora–Kigoma foundation stone on 20 Jul 2026; in Sept 2026 the Burundi link was still awaiting AfDB financing and the Rwanda link has none.
corridors.summary: An electrified standard gauge railway from the port of Dar es Salaam via Morogoro, Dodoma and Tabora to Mwanza on Lake Victoria, with a branch from Tabora to Kigoma on Lake Tanganyika and links planned to Musongati and Gitega in Burundi and to Kigali in Rwanda. It runs alongside the old metre-gauge Central Line, for freight and passengers.
corridors.strategic: Tanzania's bid to win the transit trade of Rwanda, Burundi and eastern DRC from Kenya's Northern Corridor. Turkey's Yapı Merkezi builds the trunk with European export credit agencies (Sweden, Italy, Poland) and Standard Chartered, while Chinese state firms build the Mwanza, Kigoma and Burundi lots; the Burundi branch targets Musongati's nickel.

corridors.name: East African Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP)
corridors.length_note: 296 km in Uganda and 1,147 km in Tanzania, from Kabaale (Hoima) to the Chongoleani terminal near Tanga.

cost.note: Project cost as reported in March 2025; BankTrack cites USD 5.6 bn as of July 2025. Owners provide about USD 2 bn of equity, with USD 2.4-3 bn of debt initially sought.

corridors.status_note: UNOC put the pipeline at over 90% complete in Sept 2026, with 1,414 of 1,443 km laid and buried. On 11 Oct 2026 Ugandan officials said it will be ready to take crude by mid-December 2026, but first commercial oil slipped to before end-June 2027, blamed on delayed equipment shipments from the Middle East.
corridors.summary: A buried, heated 24-inch crude oil pipeline from the Lake Albert oil fields (Tilenga and Kingfisher) in western Uganda to a marine storage terminal and jetty at Chongoleani near Tanga, Tanzania. Capacity is up to 246,000 barrels a day.
corridors.strategic: EACOP is landlocked Uganda's export route for its first oil, chosen over a route through Kenya to Lamu. Western banks and insurers have refused to fund it under climate pressure, so debt has come from African and Islamic lenders, Chinese lenders have been reported but not confirmed, and TotalEnergies and CNOOC carry most of the cost.

corridors.name: TAZARA revitalisation (Tanzania–Zambia Railway, Dar es Salaam–Kapiri Mposhi)
corridors.length_note: Dar es Salaam to New Kapiri Mposhi, Cape gauge (1,067 mm); 975 km in Tanzania, 885 km in Zambia

cost.note: CCECC's investment under the 30-year concession: about USD 1.0 bn for track, bridges and workshops and USD 0.4 bn for 32 locomotives and 762 wagons (later reports: about 34 locomotives, 760 wagons, 18 coaches). An April 2026 report values the project at USD 1.24 bn.

corridors.status_note: The line runs at a fraction of capacity while it is rebuilt. The concession with CCECC was signed on 29 Sep 2025 (some reports say Nov 2025) and launched in Lusaka on 20 Nov 2025 with China's Premier Li Qiang. In April 2026 the Chinese side said final designs were almost ready and restated a three-year build; in July 2026 CCECC was mobilising and broke ground on a training centre and control centre in Dar es Salaam. No report yet of main track works.
corridors.summary: A 1,860 km railway built with Chinese finance and technical support in 1970-75, linking Zambia's Copperbelt to the Indian Ocean port of Dar es Salaam. China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation (CCECC) will spend about USD 1.4 bn to rehabilitate track and bridges and buy new rolling stock, then run the line for 30 years. It is meant to lift freight from about 200,000 t to 2.4 Mt a year, mainly Copperbelt minerals for export.
corridors.strategic: China's flagship corridor in the region: the original line was financed by an interest-free Chinese loan, and the revival was agreed at the 2024 FOCAC summit before Xi Jinping, Samia Suluhu Hassan and Hakainde Hichilema. It is widely reported as Beijing's answer to the US/EU-backed Lobito Corridor, competing for the same Zambian and Congolese copper, with Chinese miners CMOC and Zijin reported to be taking stakes.

corridors.name: Nacala Logistics Corridor (Moatize–Malawi–Nacala railway and ports)
corridors.length_note: Railway from the Moatize coal mines (Tete) through southern Malawi to the coal terminal at Nacala-a-Velha; the World Bank describes the wider multimodal corridor, into eastern Zambia, as 1,600 km

cost.note: World Bank estimate (May 2025) of investment in the corridor over the past decade: USD 4.2 bn for the Moatize mine, new and rehabilitated railway and Nacala-a-Velha coal terminal; USD 600 m for Malawi and Mozambique rail branch lines; about USD 1 bn of public road works; plus a USD 350 m Japanese package for Nacala port

corridors.status_note: The railway and ports are in service (about 13.6 Mt of coal in 2023; a monthly record of 1.4 Mt in May 2025). In Dec 2025 Mozambique, Malawi, Zambia and DR Congo signed a ministerial declaration to extend the corridor by about 2,400 km of new railway, and on 24 Apr 2026 Zambia Railways and Nacala Logistics signed an MoU to revive the dormant Chipata–Mchinji link.
corridors.summary: A heavy-haul railway built by Vale and Mitsui from the Moatize coal basin in Mozambique's Tete province, across southern Malawi, to a deep-water coal terminal at Nacala-a-Velha, plus Nacala's general cargo port and Malawi's rail network. It carries mainly coking coal for export (capacity 18 Mt a year), plus fuel and general cargo to and from Malawi. Since April 2022 it is owned and run by Vulcan, part of India's Jindal group, as Nacala Logistics.
corridors.strategic: Japan's corridor: Japanese lenders financed the railway in 2017 and JICA rebuilt Nacala port, and at TICAD 9 (Aug 2025) Tokyo launched 'Strengthening the Global Supply Chain through Nacala Corridor Development' for Mozambique, Malawi and Zambia, aimed at minerals supply chains. A link to Zambia would give Copperbelt cargo a short route to the Indian Ocean, competing with TAZARA and Lobito.

segments.name: Moatize–Nacala-a-Velha railway (via Malawi)
segments.status_note: Inaugurated by Vale in May 2017 (new line through Malawi plus rebuilt track in Mozambique). About 13.6 Mt of coal moved in 2023; Nacala Logistics reported 1.4 Mt in May 2025 alone. Owned by Vulcan (Jindal) since April 2022.

segments.name: Nacala-a-Velha coal terminal
segments.status_note: Deep-water coal export terminal built with the railway; Nacala Logistics gives an annual shipping capacity of 18 Mt.

segments.name: Nacala general cargo and container port
segments.status_note: Redeveloped with a 2012 Japanese grant and soft-loan package of about USD 350 m (JICA yen loans in 2013 and 2015); delayed by COVID-19, fully operational by 2023.

segments.name: Malawi line Nkaya–Lilongwe–Mchinji
segments.status_note: Branch upgraded by the corridor's private sponsors (part of USD 600 m spent on branch lines). Fuel trains from Nacala to Lilongwe resumed in July 2024 after 21 years, about 15 m litres a month; first coal train reached Lilongwe the same month.

segments.name: Chipata–Mchinji link to Zambia
segments.status_note: Short cross-border line idle for years after flood damage and COVID-19. On 24 Apr 2026 Zambia Railways and Nacala Logistics (CEAR) signed an MoU to rehabilitate and operate it, targeting over 100,000 t a month. A Dec 2025 four-country declaration envisages about 2,400 km of new railway beyond Chipata; a strategic partner was due to be chosen in Q1 2026, not confirmed.

backers.name: Vulcan Resources (Jindal group)
backers.what: Bought the Moatize mine and the Nacala Logistics Corridor (railway, ports, Malawi concession) from Vale for USD 270 m plus a 10-year royalty; deal announced Dec 2021, closed April 2022. Runs it as Nacala Logistics (CDN, CLN, CEAR, VLL).

backers.name: Vale
backers.what: Built and owned the corridor with Mitsui; bought out Mitsui and prepaid about USD 2.5 bn of outstanding project finance in June 2021 before selling to Vulcan.

backers.name: Japan Bank for International Cooperation (JBIC)
backers.what: Lent USD 1.03 bn of a USD 2.73 bn project financing signed Nov 2017 (with commercial banks covered by NEXI and South Africa's ECIC); repaid early by Vale in June 2021.

backers.name: African Development Bank (AfDB)
backers.what: USD 300 m loan in the 2017 project financing; repaid early in June 2021.

backers.name: Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA)
backers.what: ODA yen loans to Mozambique for the Nacala Port Development Project: up to JPY 7.889 bn (Phase I, Mar 2013) and JPY 29.235 bn (Phase II, Jun 2015), for dredging, wharf repair, container yard and cranes.
backers.segment: Nacala general cargo and container port

backers.name: World Bank (IDA)
backers.what: USD 123.3 m IDA grant for Transport Corridors for Economic Resilience – Mozambique SOP2 (P510427): about 124 km of feeder roads, climate resilience and road safety along the Nacala corridor; appraised May 2025.

backers.name: Zambia Railways Limited
backers.what: Signed an MoU with Nacala Logistics on 24 Apr 2026 to rehabilitate and operate the Chipata–Mchinji line.

corridors.name: Maputo Development Corridor (Gauteng–Mpumalanga–Maputo)
corridors.length_note: N4 toll route from Pretoria to Maputo; the railway from Pretoria via Komatipoort and Ressano Garcia runs roughly parallel
corridors.status_note: In late September 2026 South African and Mozambican border agencies, with the World Bank, were working to clear multi-day truck queues at Lebombo/Ressano Garcia (up to 1,800 trucks a day), with a one-stop border post as the long-term aim. Maputo port handled a record 32.0 Mt in 2025, and in Feb 2026 Mozambique decided to tender the N4 concession that TRAC holds until 2028.
corridors.summary: Road, rail and port corridor from South Africa's industrial heartland (Gauteng and Mpumalanga) to the port of Maputo, via the N4 toll road, the Pretoria–Komatipoort–Ressano Garcia–Maputo railway and the Lebombo/Ressano Garcia border. It carries chrome ore, ferrochrome, coal and magnetite exports from South Africa's north-east, plus containers and citrus. The private corridor body (MCLI) also covers Eswatini.
corridors.strategic: Bottlenecks in South Africa's Transnet logistics have diverted mining exports to Maputo, which hit record volumes in 2025. The port is run by MPDC, controlled by Dubai's DP World and South Africa's Grindrod with Mozambique's CFM, under a concession extended to 2058. EU Global Gateway lists it within corridor 9 (Maputo–Gaborone–Walvis Bay), which continues west via the Trans-Kalahari road to Namibia.

named_by.list: EU Global Gateway strategic corridor 9 (Maputo–Gaborone–Walvis Bay)

segments.name: Port of Maputo (MPDC concession)
segments.status_note: Record 32.0 Mt in 2025 (+3.4%), 11.7 Mt of it by rail (+17%). Concession extended in Feb 2024 from 2033 to 2058, with nearly USD 1.1 bn of investment due by 2033. Under way: DP World container terminal expansion to 530,000 TEU, bulk terminal to 16 Mt, Grindrod's magnetite and coal terminal to 12 Mt.
funded_by: Portos e Caminhos de Ferro de Moçambique (CFM)

segments.name: Ressano Garcia railway line (Maputo–Ressano Garcia)
segments.status_note: 88 km CFM line. Doubling from Maputo to Secongene finished Sep 2024; AFD loans and an EU grant (project started July 2025, to 2030) fund doubling of the last single-track section, Movene–Ressano Garcia, a longer yard at the Ressano Garcia dry port and new signalling on the whole line.

segments.name: Pretoria–Komatipoort railway (Transnet)
segments.status_note: South African section run by Transnet Freight Rail. In Sep 2024 TFR said it could run at least 21 chrome trains a week to Maputo and that the line was under-used by chrome exporters. No newer Transnet capacity figure found.

segments.name: N4 Toll Route (Pretoria–Maputo)
segments.status_note: Cross-border toll concession held by TRAC since 1997, operating since 2000, ending in 2028. On 17 Feb 2026 Mozambique's cabinet decided to tender for a new concessionaire for its section; TRAC wants to bid. TRAC began rehabilitating 66 km between Ressano Garcia and Tchumene in June 2025.

segments.name: Lebombo / Ressano Garcia border post
segments.status_note: Chronic truck congestion: 1,339-1,734 trucks a day processed on 21-24 Sep 2026, peaks above 1,800. SARS is automating the KM7 truck staging site; a one-stop border post was discussed with the World Bank on 15-17 Sep 2026 but has no start date.

backers.name: DP World
backers.what: Dubai state-owned port group; co-owns the Maputo Port Development Company (MPDC) with Grindrod through Portus Indico and is expanding its Maputo container terminal to 530,000 TEU.

backers.name: Grindrod
backers.what: Holds 24.7% of MPDC, whose port concession was extended to 2058 in Feb 2024 with nearly USD 1.1 bn of investment due from MPDC and its shareholders by 2033; also runs the Matola coal and magnetite terminal.

backers.name: Portos e Caminhos de Ferro de Moçambique (CFM)
backers.what: Mozambique's state ports and rail company: state shareholder in MPDC and owner-operator of the Ressano Garcia line, borrowing from AFD for its doubling.

backers.name: Agence française de développement (AFD)
backers.what: Two non-sovereign loans to CFM, described as USD 133.4 m (the project summary says USD 163.4 m), for doubling Movene–Ressano Garcia and new signalling; project 2025-2030.

backers.name: European Union
backers.what: EUR 30 m grant alongside the AFD loans for the Ressano Garcia line.

backers.name: Trans African Concessions (TRAC)
backers.what: 30-year build-operate-transfer concession for the N4 signed 1997, capital value ZAR 3 bn, financed 20% equity and 80% debt from mainly South African banks, with debt guaranteed by the two governments; original sponsors Bouygues, Basil Read and Stocks & Stocks.

corridors.name: North–South Corridor (Durban–Johannesburg–Beitbridge/Kazungula–Lusaka–Lubumbashi)
corridors.length_note: No official end-to-end length found. Sections: Beitbridge–Harare 580 km, Harare–Chirundu about 350 km, Lusaka–Ndola 327 km
corridors.status_note: Zimbabwe reached financial close on the Chirundu one-stop border post upgrade in early Oct 2026 and CBZ Bank committed USD 100 m to the Harare–Chirundu road in Aug 2026. By mid-July 2026, 550 of 580 km of the Beitbridge–Harare road were upgraded and open; Zambia's Lusaka–Ndola dual carriageway was 78% complete in June 2026.
corridors.summary: One of southern Africa's main road freight routes, from the port of Durban through Johannesburg to the Zambian and Congolese Copperbelt (Kasumbalesa, Lubumbashi). It splits into two branches: through Zimbabwe via the Beitbridge and Chirundu border posts, or through Botswana via the Kazungula Bridge into Zambia. It links South Africa's ports with the Zambia–DRC Copperbelt.
corridors.strategic: A patchwork of national and donor projects rather than one sponsor: Japan (JICA) and the AfDB paid for Kazungula, South African banks and Afreximbank for Beitbridge, Zimbabwe's own budget for its highway, and a Chinese state-owned consortium builds Zambia's Lusaka–Ndola toll road. Lobito, TAZARA and Nacala are pitched as alternatives to this route and South Africa's congested ports; COMESA, EAC and SADC treat it as a Tripartite trade-facilitation corridor.

segments.name: Beitbridge border post (Zimbabwe side)
segments.status_note: Rebuilt under a 17.5-year build-operate-transfer concession by the Zimborders consortium (reported cost USD 240-300 m); the new terminal was commissioned in Sep 2022 according to Zimbabwe's Herald. Zimborders says it clears about 500-750 trucks a day.

segments.name: Beitbridge–Harare road (A4)
segments.status_note: Rehabilitation and widening by five local contractors: 550.1 of 580 km upgraded and open as of 14 July 2026; the last 31.9 km due by end-2026.

segments.name: Harare–Chirundu road (A1)
segments.status_note: Full rehabilitation estimated at about USD 900 m. CBZ Bank committed USD 100 m in Aug 2026, ring-fenced against road toll revenue; no start date for the main works reported.

segments.name: Chirundu one-stop border post upgrade (Zimbabwe–Zambia)
segments.status_note: Southern Africa's first one-stop border post (opened 2009). A PPP with the Chirundu Border Consortium to upgrade and run the Zimbabwean side reached financial close in early Oct 2026, with Standard Bank and Stanbic Bank Zimbabwe as lead arrangers; construction yet to start. Zimbabwe's cabinet earlier put the cost at USD 66.8 m.

segments.name: Kazungula Bridge and one-stop border post (Botswana–Zambia)
segments.status_note: 923 m road-rail bridge over the Zambezi replacing a ferry; opened by the presidents of Botswana and Zambia in May 2021. Total cost USD 259.3 m.

segments.name: Lusaka–Ndola dual carriageway
segments.status_note: 327 km toll road PPP signed Feb 2023, works from 2024; 78% complete on the main carriageway in June 2026, with completion expected in 2026 ahead of a 2027 deadline.

backers.name: Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA)
backers.what: ODA loans of up to JPY 8.735 bn to Botswana and JPY 2.877 bn to Zambia (signed Oct 2012) for the Kazungula Bridge, co-financed with the AfDB.
backers.segment: Kazungula Bridge and one-stop border post (Botswana–Zambia)

backers.name: African Development Bank (AfDB)
backers.what: USD 76.5 m loan for the Kazungula Bridge (project approved Dec 2011), alongside JICA, the two governments and the EU-Africa Infrastructure Trust Fund.
backers.segment: Kazungula Bridge and one-stop border post (Botswana–Zambia)

backers.name: Zimborders Consortium
backers.what: Financed, built and runs the modernised Beitbridge border post under a 17.5-year BOT concession; senior debt arranged by Absa, Nedbank, RMB, Standard Bank and Afreximbank, about USD 81 m equity; reported cost USD 240-300 m.

backers.name: Afreximbank
backers.what: Mandated lead arranger, lender and insurer in the Beitbridge border post financing.

backers.name: Government of Zimbabwe
backers.what: Funds the Beitbridge–Harare road rehabilitation from its own resources (amount not given); told a SADC ministerial round table in Feb 2025 it had committed substantial resources and planned the 350 km to Chirundu next.

backers.name: CBZ Bank
backers.what: Committed USD 100 m to the Harare–Chirundu highway in Aug 2026, part of a USD 400 m road loan facility, repaid from road toll collections.

backers.name: Standard Bank / Stanbic Bank Zimbabwe
backers.what: Lead arrangers and lenders for the Chirundu border post upgrade PPP (financial close early Oct 2026); amount not disclosed.

backers.name: Macro Ocean Investment Consortium
backers.what: Chinese state-owned firms AVIC International Project Engineering, Zhenjiang Communications Construction Group and China Railway Seventh Group; 25-year design-finance-build-operate concession (USD 650 m) signed Feb 2023, repaid from tolls. Zambia says no state money or guarantee; one project tracker says Zambian pension funds NAPSA and WCFCB provide finance.

corridors.name: Abidjan–Lagos Corridor Highway
corridors.length_note: AfDB and PIDA PAP2 prospectus figure, Bingerville (Abidjan) to Lagos; ECOWAS and the PIDA project page cite about 1,080 km. AfDB country split (2024): Côte d'Ivoire 144, Ghana 520, Togo 90, Benin 127, Nigeria 82 km, which sums to 963 km.

cost.note: Construction cost in the PIDA PAP2 prospectus; the same figure was announced as investment interest at the 2022 Africa Investment Forum. The PIDA PAP2 project page lists capex of USD 7 bn and 2026 ECOWAS coverage cites about USD 15 bn.

corridors.status_note: The board of the Abidjan-Lagos Corridor Management Authority (ALCoMA) held its first meeting in Lagos in June 2026, named a chair and admitted the AfDB as a non-voting member and lead arranger; the AfDB is discussing USD 500 m of catalytic capital. Feasibility and structuring work was 'near completion' in February 2026; no construction financing or works contract has been reported, and PIDA schedules the first construction phase for 2027-2030.
corridors.summary: A planned six-lane coastal highway of about 1,028 km from Abidjan through Accra, Lomé and Cotonou to Lagos, with eight border posts. It would upgrade West Africa's busiest trade route, which carries more than 50 million tonnes of freight a year and where trucks can take up to 17 days end to end.
corridors.strategic: An ECOWAS project with the AfDB as lead arranger and EU grants behind its studies, and the first of the EU's Global Gateway strategic corridors in Africa. It links the coastal economies and the ports that serve landlocked Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger; China built the first finished piece, the Abidjan–Grand-Bassam motorway.

segments.name: Abidjan–Grand-Bassam motorway
segments.status_note: Six-lane motorway opened to traffic in September 2015; the PIDA PAP2 prospectus counts it as the first built part of the corridor.

segments.name: Côte d'Ivoire section (Abidjan–Noé)
segments.status_note: Design studies only; no works contract reported as of June 2026.

segments.name: Ghana section (Elubo–Takoradi–Accra–Aflao)
segments.status_note: Design studies only; no works contract reported as of June 2026.

segments.name: Togo and Benin sections (Lomé–Cotonou–Kraké)
segments.status_note: Design studies only (Togo 90 km, Benin 127 km); no works contract reported as of June 2026.

segments.name: Nigeria section: Lagos–Badagry–Seme expressway rebuild
segments.status_note: The federal government is rebuilding Agbara–Badagry (24.3 km) and Badagry–Seme (21.8 km) as a six-lane road, described as part of the ECOWAS Lagos–Abidjan corridor; the first section was due in April 2025 and the stretch was listed for commissioning on 31 May 2025. No later update was found.

backers.name: African Development Bank (AfDB)
backers.what: Mandated lead arranger for the highway's financing (with EBID); has put about USD 25 m into technical assistance and preparation, and in June 2026 was discussing USD 500 m of catalytic capital (not committed).

backers.name: European Union
backers.what: EUR 9.1 m grant, channelled through the AfDB, for the feasibility and detailed design studies (2019 agreement; total study package USD 22.7 m).

backers.name: European Union
backers.what: Reported EUR 45 m commitment at the Abidjan business forum (30 March-1 April 2026), shared between the Abidjan–Lagos and Abidjan–Ouagadougou corridors (Global Gateway support project GGSP-CALAO).

backers.name: China Exim Bank
backers.what: USD 114.77 m loan to Côte d'Ivoire for the Abidjan–Grand-Bassam motorway (signed October 2011).

backers.name: China Machinery Engineering Corporation (CMEC)
backers.what: Built the Abidjan–Grand-Bassam motorway, completed in June 2015.

backers.name: Federal Government of Nigeria
backers.what: Paying for the Agbara–Badagry–Seme rebuild under a NGN 71 bn contract first awarded in 2018 (NGN 50 bn paid by early 2025).

corridors.name: African Atlantic Gas Pipeline (Nigeria–Morocco Gas Pipeline)
corridors.length_note: ONHYM's 2026 figure for the hybrid offshore-onshore route through 13 countries; earlier figures range from 5,660 to 7,000 km. The Moroccan section is 2,220 km (1,830 km onshore, 390 km offshore), running from the Mauritanian maritime border through Western Sahara.

cost.note: Whole-project estimate cited by ONHYM; one 2026 report gives about USD 27 bn.

corridors.status_note: ECOWAS heads of state signed the intergovernmental agreement in Freetown on 19 July 2026; Morocco and Mauritania are to sign separately later in 2026. Feasibility and FEED studies are complete, but no financing is committed and the final investment decision, targeted for Q4 2026, was still pending at end-September 2026; ONHYM expects construction from 2028 and first gas in 2031.
corridors.summary: A planned 48-inch gas pipeline from Nigeria along the Atlantic coast to Morocco, with up to 30 bcm a year of capacity, about half for Morocco and export to Europe through the Maghreb-Europe pipeline and the rest for West African markets. It is to be built in independently financed sections, starting with a northern section bringing Senegal and Mauritania gas to Morocco; a project company in Morocco (ONHYM-NNPC joint venture) and a governing authority in Abuja are still to be set up.
corridors.strategic: Morocco's rival to Algeria's Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline: both promise Nigerian gas to Europe. The Moroccan section runs through Western Sahara (Dakhla, Boujdour), whose status is disputed, and the UAE has said it will help fund the project.

segments.name: Main line, Nigeria to Morocco
segments.status_note: Intergovernmental agreement signed by ECOWAS states on 19 July 2026; FID targeted Q4 2026, first gas 2031.
funded_by: Office National des Hydrocarbures et des Mines (ONHYM)

segments.name: Moroccan section, Dakhla–Ouazzane (phase 1B)
segments.status_note: Environmental study published July 2026: 2,220 km with four compressor stations (Boujdour, Tan-Tan, Agadir, Safi) and a link to the Maghreb-Europe pipeline in Ouazzane province; construction (about 2.5 years) to start after the FID. A 2025 plan to start works on a first Nador–Dakhla portion that summer did not materialise.
funded_by: Office National des Hydrocarbures et des Mines (ONHYM)

segments.name: West African Gas Pipeline (existing, Nigeria–Ghana)
segments.status_note: Existing line from Nigeria to Ghana; reported plans for the first phase would extend it west to San Pédro in Côte d'Ivoire (sources differ on phase numbering).

backers.name: Nigerian National Petroleum Company (NNPC)
backers.what: Co-developer; to be partner with ONHYM in the project company that will lead execution, financing and construction.

backers.name: Office National des Hydrocarbures et des Mines (ONHYM)
backers.what: Co-developer and executing agency for the FEED studies; to be partner with NNPC in the project company based in Morocco.

backers.name: OPEC Fund
backers.what: USD 14.3 m loan to Morocco, approved September 2021, co-financing FEED phase II surveys for the North Area (Senegal, Mauritania, Morocco); total study cost USD 90.1 m.

backers.name: Islamic Development Bank (IsDB)
backers.what: Service Ijara financing to ONHYM for FEED-phase work (environmental and social impact assessment, land acquisition study, audit); press reports put IsDB support at USD 15.4 m for Morocco's share and USD 29.7 m for Nigeria's, not confirmed by the bank.

backers.name: United Arab Emirates
backers.what: Agreed with Morocco to help fund the pipeline through a mix of capital investment, concessional loans and grants; no amount disclosed.

corridors.name: Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline (Nigeria–Niger–Algeria, NIGAL)
corridors.length_note: Warri (Nigeria) to Hassi R'Mel (Algeria): about 1,037 km in Nigeria, 841 km in Niger and 2,310-2,424 km in Algeria, of which 1,210 km is new line to the existing network at Aoulef; the country figures do not sum exactly to the total.

cost.note: Whole-pipeline estimate cited in 2026; other estimates run from USD 10 bn.

corridors.status_note: Sonatrach began welding the new 1,210 km Algerian section at Aoulef (Adrar) on 4 June 2026, the day after the three partners adopted an updated feasibility study. Niger said topographic surveys of its 841 km section would start in early October 2026, with works in early 2027 with Sonatrach; the Nigerian section has no date and no final investment decision or financing for the whole line has been announced.
corridors.summary: A planned 30 bcm/yr gas pipeline from Warri in Nigeria's Niger Delta through Niger to Algeria's Hassi R'Mel hub, where gas would join Algeria's network and its export pipelines to Europe. Nigeria's 614 km Ajaokuta–Kaduna–Kano (AKK) line, phase one of the Trans-Nigeria Gas Pipeline, is the first step on the Nigerian side.
corridors.strategic: Algeria's rival to the Morocco-backed Atlantic pipeline for Nigerian gas to Europe; it moved after Algiers and Niger's military government repaired relations in 2026. Algeria is building its own section and has said Sonatrach will also finance and build the Niger section.

segments.name: Algerian section, Niger border–Aoulef (new build)
segments.status_note: First welds made at Aoulef on 4 June 2026; the new line follows the Trans-Saharan Road corridor from the Niger border and ties into the existing network toward Hassi R'Mel.

segments.name: Niger section, with the link south to Kano
segments.status_note: Topographic surveys announced for early October 2026, works for early 2027. Algeria's president said Sonatrach will finance and build it; Niger-side reporting in September 2026 said financing was not yet published.

segments.name: Ajaokuta–Kaduna–Kano (AKK) pipeline, Nigeria
segments.status_note: NNPC's July 2026 report (published September) put AKK at 95%, with early gas to Abuja targeted in 2026; main-line welding and the River Niger crossing were finished by December 2025. Earlier targets (2022, Q1 2025, Q1 2026) were missed.

geometry.name: Trans Nigeria Gas Pipeline · Phase 1: Ajaokuta–Kaduna–Kano Pipeline (AKK Pipeline)

backers.name: Sonatrach
backers.what: Algeria's state energy company; building the 1,210 km Algerian section and, per Algeria's president, to finance and build the Niger section. Sonatrach and NNPC are to hold 90% of the project, SONIDEP 10%.

backers.name: Nigerian National Petroleum Company (NNPC)
backers.what: Co-developer of the trunk line and owner of the AKK pipeline; funded AKK works from its own resources while Chinese loan disbursements were delayed (from 2021).

backers.name: SONIDEP
backers.what: Niger's state oil company; partner in the project with a 10% share.
backers.segment: Niger section, with the link south to Kano

backers.name: Bank of China and ICBC
backers.what: USD 2.46 bn syndicated loan to NNPC for AKK (2020), with a Nigerian sovereign guarantee and Sinosure cover; Bank of China reportedly withheld disbursements in 2021.

backers.name: Oilserv
backers.what: Led the consortium (with Oando and China First Highway Engineering) building the Ajaokuta–Abuja segment of AKK.

backers.name: China Petroleum Pipeline Engineering (CPP)
backers.what: Built the northern part of AKK with Brentex Petroleum Services.

corridors.name: Niger–Benin Oil Pipeline (Agadem–Sèmè) and the Cotonou–Niamey corridor
corridors.length_note: AidData figure from the loan record, of which 1,293 km in Niger; press reports cite 1,930-2,000 km.

cost.note: Niger section only (1,293 km), financed 80:20 debt to equity; no sourced figure for the whole line.

corridors.status_note: Exporting through the Sèmè offshore terminal since 2024, after a May-August 2024 halt over the Benin-Niger border dispute and a June 2024 rebel attack. On 18 May 2026 Niger and CNPC agreed to cut the transport tariff from USD 27 to 15 a barrel and give Niger a 45% stake in operator WAPCO; in August 2026 Sonatrach and SONIDEP jointly sold a Nigerien cargo loaded at the Benin terminal. The land border, closed by Niger since 2023, was still under talks to reopen in June 2026.
corridors.summary: A crude oil pipeline built by CNPC from the Agadem oilfields in eastern Niger to an offshore loading terminal about 15 km off Sèmè-Kpodji, east of Cotonou, designed for about 90,000-110,000 barrels a day. It is landlocked Niger's export outlet for crude; the parallel Cotonou–Niamey railway, begun by Bolloré, stopped after a 140 km Niamey–Dosso stretch that has never carried traffic.
corridors.strategic: China's main asset in the Sahel: CNPC built, financed and runs the line through its subsidiary WAPCO, and Niger's oil revenue depends on transit through Benin, a neighbour it fell out with after the July 2023 coup. The route matches the EU's Global Gateway Cotonou–Niamey corridor.

named_by.list: PIDA PAP2 (2021-2030): Abidjan–Ouagadougou–Niamey–Cotonou–Lomé Regional Rail Loop (covers the Niamey–Cotonou railway, 1,101 km)

segments.name: Pipeline, Agadem–Sèmè
segments.status_note: Niger section completed November 2023; exports running since August 2024 after the 2024 halt; tariff cut agreed May 2026.

segments.name: Sèmè-Kpodji offshore loading terminal
segments.status_note: Loading crude for export; a Sonatrach-SONIDEP cargo was loaded there in August 2026.

segments.name: Benin–Niger land border (Malanville–Gaya)
segments.status_note: Closed by Niger since August 2023; Presidents Wadagni and Tiani agreed on 2 June 2026 to work toward reopening and an expert committee reported on 21 June 2026, with Niamey setting security preconditions. No reopening confirmed since.

segments.name: Niamey–Dosso railway (Cotonou–Niamey line)
segments.status_note: About 140 km built by Bolloré and inaugurated in January 2016 but never used for traffic; Benin courts halted the Benin side after a challenge by Petrolin, and Bolloré gave up the rail loop in a July 2022 settlement with Benin and Niger. The track is now badly degraded.

backers.name: China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC)
backers.what: Built and operates the pipeline through its subsidiary West African Oil Pipeline Company (WAPCO); under the May 2026 deal it cut the tariff to USD 15 a barrel and agreed USD 1 bn of upstream investment.

backers.name: CNPC Finance (HK)
backers.what: Loan of about USD 1.04 bn to WAPCo-Niger (then 85% CNPC, 15% Niger) for the Niger section; face value not published.

backers.name: China Petroleum Pipeline Engineering (CPP)
backers.what: Contractor for the Niger section (with CNPC's planning institute CPPEI); works started September 2019 and ended November 2023.

backers.name: China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC)
backers.what: USD 400 m advance to Niger's government against future crude sales shipped through the pipeline, signed April 2024 (reported 7% interest, repayable within a year).

backers.name: Government of Niger
backers.what: Agreed in May 2026 to take a 45% stake in WAPCO (agreement in principle); Ecofin says the state previously held none, while AidData lists 15% in WAPCo-Niger.

backers.name: Bolloré
backers.what: Won the Cotonou–Niamey rail contract in 2013 and built the Niamey–Dosso track (2014-2016); withdrew from the rail loop in a July 2022 settlement.

corridors.name: Trans-Saharan Highway (Algiers–Lagos)
corridors.length_note: Main Algiers–Lagos axis (AfDB); the full network with branches to Tunisia, Mali and Chad is 9,022 km.
corridors.status_note: At its 77th session in Algiers on 8-9 June 2026 the Trans-Saharan Road Liaison Committee (CLRT) said the network is over 90% built and the Algiers–Lagos axis almost complete; the last unpaved stretch of the main axis, PK0–Assamaka on the Niger side of the Algerian border, was in works for completion in 2026. About 400 km remain on the Mali branch and two sections (97 and 85 km) in Chad; in July 2026 EBID approved USD 260 m for a 123 km section in Nigeria.
corridors.summary: A road network first proposed by UNECA in 1962, running from Algiers across the Sahara via Ghardaïa, In Salah, Tamanrasset, Arlit and Agadez to Kano and Lagos, with branches to Tunisia, to Mali and to N'Djamena. A trans-Saharan fibre-optic backbone is being laid along it: Niger finished its 1,031 km in November 2025 and the Algeria–Niger link was launched at Assamaka in October 2026.
corridors.strategic: Algeria's road to the Sahel: it gives Niger, Mali and Chad access to Algerian ports and the Mediterranean, and Algiers now also builds road sections in Chad. No permanent body has the powers to coordinate it (UNCTAD wants the liaison committee, CLRT, turned into one), and its member states sit in different regional blocs.

segments.status_note: Paved throughout. The Abuja–Kaduna–Kano dual carriageway is being rebuilt in concrete: first 118 km section finished June 2026, last 164 km due November 2026. EBID approved USD 260 m for a 123 km Trans-Saharan section in Nigeria on 6 July 2026.

segments.status_note: Long delays on contracts in Chad; Algerian contractors were to start two remaining sections of 97 km and 85 km in June 2026. The World Bank's Chad Connectivity and Integration Project (USD 170 m, 2025) aims to finish Chad's section.

corridors.name: Addis Ababa–Djibouti Railway and the Doraleh port complex
corridors.length_note: Sebeta (Addis Ababa) to Nagad (Djibouti), as given by CREC and by FS Engineering/Italferr; AidData records give between 750 and 759 km.

cost.note: China Exim Bank buyer's credits only, both signed in May 2013: USD 2.49 bn to Ethiopia (three tranches covering about 70% of the Ethiopian EPC contracts and rolling stock) and USD 491.8 m to Djibouti for its 100 km section. A total build cost of about USD 4 bn is often quoted, but we found no primary source for it.

corridors.status_note: In commercial service since January 2018 and run since May 2024 by the bi-national Ethio-Djibouti Railway (EDR) after the Chinese builders handed over. In February 2026 the two governments agreed to rail-link the Doraleh Multipurpose Port and the HDTL oil terminal by November 2026, and EDR said in July 2026 that the line now carries 50% of Ethiopia's exports and 24% of its imports. Ethiopia announced a debt-treatment resolution with China in April 2026.
corridors.summary: A 752.7 km electrified standard-gauge railway from Sebeta, on the edge of Addis Ababa, to Nagad near the Doraleh port complex in Djibouti, built by CREC and CCECC with China Exim Bank loans. It carries freight and passengers between landlocked Ethiopia and Djibouti, whose ports handle about 90% of Ethiopia's trade.
corridors.strategic: China's flagship Belt and Road railway in Africa. Both borrowers fell behind on repayments and their loans were rescheduled (Ethiopia 2018, Djibouti 2019-2020); Ethiopia's China debt is now being treated under the G20 Common Framework. Ethiopia's dependence on this one route to Djibouti drives Abiy Ahmed's push for a Red Sea outlet of its own, which he restated when sworn in for a new term on 5 October 2026.

segments.name: Ethiopian section, Sebeta–Adama–Mieso–Dire Dawa–Dewele
segments.status_note: CREC built Sebeta–Adama–Mieso and CCECC built Mieso–Dewele; commercial operation began 1 January 2018. EDR had 1,100 wagons and 35 electric locomotives in January 2026 and plans to double both by end-2026.

segments.name: Djibouti section, Dewele/Ali Sabieh–Nagad
segments.status_note: About 100 km, financed by a USD 491.8 m China Exim loan to Djibouti (2013); its grace period and maturity were extended under a 2019 MoU and a restructuring signed in September 2020.

segments.name: Doraleh Multipurpose Port and Doraleh Container Terminal
segments.status_note: The Doraleh Multipurpose Port opened in May 2017 and is owned by Port de Djibouti SA (23.5% China Merchants Port Holdings). Djibouti seized the neighbouring Doraleh Container Terminal from DP World in February 2018; the legal fight is unresolved, with awards for DP World and an LCIA ruling against its damages claim reported in September 2025.

segments.name: Rail links to Doraleh Multipurpose Port and the HDTL oil terminal
segments.status_note: Agreed by the Ethio-Djibouti Joint Railway Commission on 17 February 2026 with a November 2026 target. Only the SGTD container terminal is rail-linked today; DMP is reached by a 1.9 km truck shuttle. EDR is to build the ~3 km HDTL link; a 17 km line to Damerjog liquid bulk port is also planned (USD 90 m study estimate).

corridors.name: Berbera Corridor (Berbera port–Hargeisa–Wajaale/Togochale–Ethiopia)
corridors.length_note: No official length found; the Berbera–Hargeisa–Wajaale/Togochale road is reported at about 234-250 km.

cost.note: DP World's commitment of up to USD 442 m to develop and expand Berbera port under its 2016 concession; excludes the road upgrades paid by the UAE (ADFD) and the UK.

corridors.status_note: The port's new 500,000 TEU terminal has run since June 2021, but a DP World official said in September 2026 that Berbera works at about 30% of capacity because the expected Ethiopian cargo has not come. Ethiopia's January 2024 MoU with Somaliland has not been implemented, and on 12 January 2026 Somalia's federal government annulled its agreements with the UAE, including on Berbera; Somaliland rejected the move.
corridors.summary: A port-and-road corridor from DP World's Berbera port on the Gulf of Aden through Hargeisa to the Ethiopian border at Wajaale/Togochale, meant to give Ethiopia a second sea outlet besides Djibouti. Berbera lies in Somaliland, a self-declared state that Somalia considers part of its territory and that only Israel recognises (since 26 December 2025); it is coded here as Somalia (SO).
corridors.strategic: A UAE port play (DP World, with UK development money) that competes with Djibouti for Ethiopian transit trade. It sits at the centre of Horn of Africa rivalries: Ethiopia's January 2024 MoU offered Somaliland recognition in exchange for coastal access, Turkey's Ankara Declaration of December 2024 returned Ethiopia to talks with Somalia on sea access under Somali sovereignty, and Israel's recognition of Somaliland has raised the stakes.

segments.name: Berbera port, new container terminal
segments.status_note: Phase 1 opened in June 2021: 400 m quay, 17 m draft, capacity raised from 150,000 to 500,000 TEU a year. A phase 2 quay extension to 1,000 m and 2 m TEU was announced as under way in 2021 but is still described as planned in 2026; the port ran at about 30% of capacity in September 2026.

segments.name: Berbera–Hargeisa–Wajaale road (Berbera Corridor road)
segments.status_note: Upgrade of the 234 km road began in 2019, funded by the UAE and the UK; it was 85% complete in December 2021 with completion planned for end-2022. The first bridge opened in March 2022. We found no dated confirmation that the last section to Wajaale was finished.

segments.name: Hargeisa bypass
segments.status_note: 22.5 km two-lane bypass that takes corridor trucks around Hargeisa; completed in 2023 with UK funding through TradeMark Africa.

segments.name: Ethiopian side, Togochale–Jigjiga–Dire Dawa–Addis Ababa
segments.status_note: DP World and Ethiopia's transport ministry signed an MoU in May 2021 to develop the Ethiopian side, with up to USD 1 bn of logistics investment envisaged over 10 years. We found no works under it; the roads exist, but Ethiopian cargo via Berbera is still small (September 2026).

corridors.name: Simandou Trans-Guinean Railway and Morebaya ports
corridors.length_note: Dual-track main line built by WCS (Rio Tinto, July 2024). With the ~70 km SimFer spur and ~16 km WCS spur the system is 'more than 600 km'; other reports give 600-670 km.

cost.note: SimFer's funding of the rail and port infrastructure only: USD 3.5 bn for its own 70 km spur and transhipment port plus USD 3.0 bn toward the WCS-built main line, WCS spur and barge port (SimFer funds 34% of the WCS scope during construction). WCS's own spending is not published. SimFer's whole project, mine included, is USD 11.6 bn.

corridors.status_note: First ore left Morebaya in December 2025 after a start-of-operations ceremony on 11 November 2025. Rio Tinto says full rail commissioning was reached in Q1 2026, 2.2 Mt was shipped to China in H1 2026 (2026 guidance 5-10 Mt) and its own port was 85% complete in July 2026. The line carries only iron ore so far: it is designed as multi-user, and the operator CTG began building 10 passenger and freight stations in April 2026 for service by end-2026.
corridors.summary: A heavy-haul railway across Guinea from the Simandou iron ore range in the south-east (WCS blocks 1-2 near Kérouané, Rio Tinto SimFer blocks 3-4 in Beyla prefecture) to two new export ports at Morebaya in Forécariah prefecture. It is built to carry up to 120 Mt a year of iron ore and is meant to add passenger and general freight trains.
corridors.strategic: Opens one of the world's largest high-grade iron ore deposits, with the ore going mainly to China; Chinese state and private firms (Baowu, Chinalco, Winning, Weiqiao) hold most of the project alongside Rio Tinto. Guinea's state holds 15% of the rail and port company and takes full ownership after 35 years of operation.

segments.name: Trans-Guinean main line, Morebaya–Kérouané
segments.status_note: 536 km dual-track line built by WCS, with tunnels in Kindia (11.8 km) and Mamou (8.95 km) prefectures; full rail commissioning achieved in Q1 2026. Owned and operated by the Compagnie du TransGuinéen (CTG).

segments.name: SimFer spur to Simandou blocks 3-4
segments.status_note: About 70 km spur (72 km per Guinéenews) built by China Railway Construction Corporation; main structure finished in September 2025, and SimFer ore is now railed along it to the main line.

segments.name: WCS barge port, Morebaya
segments.status_note: 60 Mt/yr barge port; the first shipment left in December 2025, and SimFer ore is shipped through it until SimFer's own port is finished.

segments.name: SimFer transhipment-vessel port, Morebaya
segments.status_note: 60 Mt/yr transhipment-vessel port, 85% complete in July 2026, with commissioning of key infrastructure targeted through 2026.

backers.what: Developer of blocks 1-2; built the 536 km main line, its 16 km spur and the barge port. Owned 51% by Winning International Group and Weiqiao Aluminium (China Hongqiao Group) and 49% by China Baowu

corridors.name: Douala/Kribi–N'Djamena Corridor
corridors.length_note: No official end-to-end length found. Rail Douala–Yaoundé–Ngaoundéré (rehabilitation covers 238 km Douala–Yaoundé and 330 km Bélabo–Ngaoundéré), then road to N'Djamena; the planned rail extension is 843-997 km depending on the route.

cost.note: World Bank Cameroon-Chad Transport Corridor project (P167798), approved February 2022: Douala–Yaoundé rail rehabilitation and signalling (USD 368 m), road works mainly in Chad (USD 389 m), the Ngaoundéré rail/road platform and trade facilitation; USD 538 m of it is IDA money. Excludes the EIB/EU/AFD Bélabo–Ngaoundéré rail works, the AfDB Ngaoundéré–Garoua road and Kribi port.

corridors.status_note: The rail-road route carries Chad's trade, but upgrades are slow: on 29 September 2026 Cameroon's transport minister told Camrail to speed up the World Bank-funded Douala–Yaoundé rail contracts (rail works expected 2027-2030), and no lot of the AfDB-funded Ngaoundéré–Garoua road was above 5% done in September 2026. The Ngaoundéré–N'Djamena railway is still unagreed: Cameroon picked a western route in June 2026, and Chad said no route had been validated.
corridors.summary: The main supply route of landlocked Chad: cargo lands at Douala (or the new deep-water port at Kribi), Camrail's metre-gauge line carries it via Yaoundé to the railhead at Ngaoundéré, and trucks cover the rest to N'Djamena, either south via Touboro and Moundou or north via Garoua, Maroua and Kousséri. A rail extension from Ngaoundéré to N'Djamena has been studied for years.
corridors.strategic: Mostly Western and multilateral money (World Bank, EIB/EU, AFD, AfDB) under the EU's Global Gateway corridor 5, while China financed and built Kribi port and Chinese contractors build the roads. Gulf players are moving in: the UAE's Etihad Rail has MoUs with Chad (May 2025) and Cameroon to update the railway study and raise funds, and AD Ports took a Douala terminal concession in February 2026.

segments.name: Port of Douala
segments.status_note: Cameroon's main port and Chad's usual gateway. In February 2026 AD Ports Group and two other UAE investors took 60% of a 30-year concession for a new 4 Mt/yr dry bulk terminal, to be built 2026-2028.

segments.name: Kribi deep-water port
segments.status_note: First container terminal opened in 2018; a second terminal with a 715 m quay was launched on 9 May 2025, lifting capacity above 1 m TEU a year. Built by China Harbour Engineering Company with China Exim loans; run by Kribi Conteneurs Terminal (AGL, CMA CGM, CHEC).

segments.name: Camrail line Douala–Yaoundé–Bélabo–Ngaoundéré
segments.status_note: In service under Camrail's concession. Renewal of 238 km Douala–Yaoundé (World Bank, XAF 152 bn) and 330 km Bélabo–Ngaoundéré (EIB, EU, AFD, XAF 167.3 bn) went to tender from late 2025; works are expected from H1 2027 to 2030.

segments.name: Road Ngaoundéré–Touboro–Moundou–N'Djamena
segments.status_note: Rehabilitation of Chad's 596 km N'Djamena–Moundou–Koutéré road is the core of the World Bank/EIB/EU support; in May 2025 the World Bank reported work on the first 50 km and better traffic between N'Djamena and Moundou after maintenance.

segments.name: Road Ngaoundéré–Garoua (northern route)
segments.status_note: Reconstruction of 246 km, financed by an AfDB loan signed in March 2025 and split into five lots, all won by Chinese contractors. Works started in 2026, but no lot was above 5% physical progress at a 23 September 2026 review.

segments.name: Ngaoundéré–N'Djamena railway extension
segments.status_note: An AfDB-funded feasibility study (CPCS/Zutari) was finished in 2024 with three 800+ km options. On 5 June 2026 Cameroon's presidency picked the western route via Garoua, Maroua and Kousséri (997 km, about XAF 4,829 bn, drawn here); Chad said on 11 June that no route was validated and prefers a southern one via Moundou (about 843 km). Etihad Rail (UAE) is to update the study and seek financing.

corridors.name: Morocco's Atlantic Initiative for the Sahel and Dakhla Atlantic port
corridors.length_note: No route to the Sahel has been defined; the Tiznit–Dakhla expressway alone is 1,055 km.

cost.note: Dakhla Atlantic port only, as reported by CNN. Morocco's Ministry of Equipment and Water figures cited by The North Africa Post put it at over USD 1 bn (MAD 12.5-13 bn); a 2021 estimate was nearly USD 1.4 bn.

corridors.status_note: Dakhla Atlantic port was 62% complete in June 2026 and is due for completion at end-2028, with operations from 2029. The Tiznit–Dakhla expressway has been fully open since January 2025, and on 21 September 2026 Morocco and Mauritania signed a framework agreement to rehabilitate and widen the 480 km Nouadhibou–Nouakchott road. We found no defined or financed route onward to Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger or Chad.
corridors.summary: Announced by King Mohammed VI in November 2023, the initiative offers Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger and Chad the use of Moroccan roads, ports and railways to reach the Atlantic, centred on a new deep-water port near Dakhla. Dakhla is in Western Sahara, a disputed territory that the UN lists as non-self-governing: Morocco controls most of it and calls it its southern provinces, while the Polisario Front seeks independence. The route south crosses it into Mauritania.
corridors.strategic: Morocco's bid to become the Sahel juntas' outlet to the sea, as an alternative to the Gulf of Guinea ports they now use, and to win backing for its claim to Western Sahara (Mali endorsed Morocco's autonomy plan in July 2026 while reaffirming support for the initiative). The UAE signed a ports investment MoU in December 2023 that Morocco says covers Dakhla Atlantique, but no Emirati money for the port has been confirmed.

segments.name: Dakhla Atlantic port (Ntirift)
segments.status_note: 62% complete in June 2026 (1.3 km sea bridge 85%, breakwaters 45%); built since 2021 by SGTM and Somagec for the Ministry of Equipment and Water, about 40 km north of Dakhla; land platforms and the first quay are due by end-2026 and the whole port by end-2028.

segments.name: Tiznit–Dakhla expressway
segments.status_note: 1,055 km expressway (about USD 1 bn) via Guelmim, Tan-Tan and Laâyoune; the last stretch opened on 10 January 2025. Morocco named it after Donald Trump in July 2026.

segments.name: Dakhla–Guerguerat–Nouadhibou–Nouakchott road
segments.status_note: Framework agreement signed in Rabat on 21 September 2026 to rehabilitate and widen the 480 km Nouadhibou–Nouakchott road, called a key corridor of the Atlantic Initiative; cost and financing not disclosed.

segments.name: Smara–Amgala–Bir Moghrein road and border crossing
segments.status_note: 93 km road (MAD 49.72 m) to a second Morocco–Mauritania crossing at Amgala, 95% built and announced to open in October 2025; we found no confirmation that it has opened.

backers.name: Government of Morocco
backers.what: Owner of the Dakhla Atlantic port project through the Ministry of Equipment and Water; built the Tiznit–Dakhla expressway and the Smara–Amgala road

backers.name: SGTM
backers.what: Building Dakhla Atlantic port with Somagec since 2021, after beating Archirodon, Eiffage and Arab Contractors in the tender

backers.name: Somagec
backers.what: Building Dakhla Atlantic port with SGTM since 2021
